### Prerequisites

Before you continue, read the two texts this lesson builds on: **When size matters** (<htcite0>), where we learned to measure an object in one direction with a ruler, and **Comparing in more than one direction** (<htcite1>), where we repeated that measurement in a second direction. This lesson adds the third direction.

source.page: Comparing in more than one direction

text.text:
### Introduction

We have already learned how to measure in two different directions. In **When size matters** we measured the length of an object along a line (<htcite0>), and in **Comparing in more than one direction** we measured length and height and compared both results (<htcite1>). But measuring in two directions is still only part of the comparison: an object can match another in length and height and still be different in the direction we have not measured yet.

Before we continue, look around you. Choose an object near you — a box, a book, a brick or a piece of furniture — and look at it carefully.

source.page: Comparing in more than one direction

text.text:
Reflection 1: How many directions?

We already learned to measure in two different directions. Is that enough to describe the size of the object you just observed? Do you know anything that has fewer than three dimensions?

Every solid object around us extends in three directions: length, width and height. These three directions are called the **three dimensions**. The third direction is the one we have not measured yet, and it is the subject of this text.

Before you continue, try to find an example. A shadow on a wall, a drawing on a sheet of paper or a point on a map can help you think about objects that have only one or two dimensions.

### Remembering one direction

In **When size matters** (<htcite0>) we measured an object in a single direction. We placed the object along the ruler so that one end matched the **0** mark, kept it straight, and read the number where the other end stopped. That number was the measure of the object in that direction. Two objects that stop at the same mark are **equal in one direction**.

The method does not change when we measure a string. A string is long in one direction, so a single ruler is enough. Let us repeat the measurement and read the result.

#### Practice

Below there is one blue string. Use the **+** and **−** buttons to make it longer or shorter, and watch the ruler under it. The sentence below the string tells you its length in the direction of the ruler.

1
The blue string measures {la} in the direction of the ruler.

### Remembering two directions

In **Comparing in more than one direction** (<htcite0>) we repeated the same method in a second direction. To measure **length**, we placed the object along a horizontal ruler; to measure **height**, we placed it along a vertical ruler. We then compared the two measures. We also saw that a square is the shape whose length and height are equal.

The steps are the same as before: choose the direction, start at **0**, keep the object straight, and read the mark where it ends. Let us practice with one square.

text.text:
#### Practice

Below there is one blue shape. Use the **+** and **−** buttons to change its length and its height. The rulers show the two measures. Make the shape a square: the length and the height must be equal. Read the sentence that appears below.

1LengthHeight
The blue square has length {l1} and height {h1}. It is a square because the two measures are equal.The blue shape has length {l1} and height {h1}. It is not a square yet because the two measures are different.

### Measuring in three directions

Now we add the third direction. Length, width and height are the three dimensions of a solid object. A **cube** is a solid object whose length, width and height are all equal.

To measure a cube, we do not need a new method. We choose a direction, place one edge of the cube along the ruler so that it starts at **0**, keep that edge straight, and read the mark where it ends. Then we repeat the same step for the other two directions:

1. **Length**: measure the front edge, from left to right.
2. **Width**: measure the side edge, from front to back.
3. **Height**: measure the vertical edge, from bottom to top.

The three measures are the three dimensions of the cube. Two cubes are **fully equal** only when all three measures match. If only one or two measures match, the cubes are equal in those directions but different in the others.

**Figure 1** shows a cube and three rulers, one for each direction. Each ruler starts at 0 and stops at the measure of its edge.
LengthWidthHeight
Figure 1: A cube measured in the three directions: length, width and height.

#### Practice

Below there are two cubes of different sizes. Use the **+** and **−** buttons to change the length, the width and the height of each cube. The numbers beside the edges show the three measures.

Make the two cubes **fully equal**: all three measures must match. Read the sentence that appears below.

Cube 1LengthWidthHeight
Cube 2LengthWidthHeight
Cube 1 and cube 2 are fully equal: they have the same length ({l1}), the same width ({w1}) and the same height ({h1}).Cube 1 and cube 2 are not fully equal yet: the lengths are {l1} and {l2}, the widths are {w1} and {w2}, and the heights are {h1} and {h2}. Make all three measures match.

### Conclusion

In this text we completed the comparison of solid objects. We began by remembering how to measure **one direction** with a ruler. Then we remembered how to measure **two directions**, length and height, and how to compare both measures. Finally, we added the **third direction**: length, width and height are the three dimensions of a solid object, and a cube is the object whose three measures are equal.

To measure a cube we follow the same steps as always: choose a direction, start at 0, keep the edge straight and read the mark where it ends. We repeat this for all three directions. The practice showed that two cubes are fully equal only when all three measures match.

Now you can also answer the question from the introduction: a shadow, a drawing or a point has fewer than three dimensions, but the objects around us have three. Measuring in all three gives us a complete description of their size.
